extracted.intended_audience: high-school journalism students, student newspaper editors, and journalism teachers/advisers
extracted.subtask_description: A practical high-school textbook describing principles, forms, and classroom exercises for reporting, writing, editing, and producing a school newspaper (news leads, headlines, features, editorials, interviews, make-up, advertising, proofs, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of News / News Values
rubrics_metrics.description: For purposes of high school journalism, whatever happens of immediate interest is news. Reporters must 'look for the New, the Strange, the Picturesque, the Unexpected.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and mini-models illustrate each value (e.g., 'The New' — Lady Mary Heath's gear; 'The Strange' — botany discovery; 'The Picturesque' — explorers; 'The Unexpected' — oil discovery). Guidance: be a keen observer; sense the new, strange, picturesque, unexpected in the high school environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth, Accuracy, Objectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: The news story must be an accurate, truthful, objective narrative — the reporter should deal only with facts, not with personal opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cautions explicitly stated: 'Never give an opinion.' 'Never make a comment.' 'Never use the first person...to mean the reporter.' Only established journalists with bylines may sometimes use first person. The reporter must remain out of the picture.

rubrics_metrics.name: News Story Structure: Lead then Body
rubrics_metrics.description: Every news story must consist of two parts: the lead (opening sentence that gives the salient facts) and the body (detailed account which unravels the facts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasons: reader should get gist at a glance; compositors cut from the bottom — the beginning must contain the summary. In well-constructed stories, least necessary details are at the end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead: Purpose and Tests
rubrics_metrics.description: The opening sentence (lead) must give the salient facts and 'sum up the news in a nutshell.' It is to the news story what the topic sentence is to a paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lead elements: condensed news, salient facts. Tests: does it give the gist? Exercises and keys provided for lead writing. Leads should be practiced daily and read aloud in class to build skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cautions for News Writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific prohibitions and cautions for reporters: do not give opinions, do not comment, avoid first-person reporting, maintain truth and accuracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Additional cautions across chapters: avoid vague words, generalities; be objective; in news stories keep the reporter out of the narrative; for features and other forms different allowances apply (e.g., literary tone).

rubrics_metrics.name: Headline Writing Principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Headlines (heads) should be based on the lead, convey the key line/punch, be economical of words, and follow technical conventions (units, decks, cross-line, drop-line, tense, figures, punctuation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance includes: do's and don'ts, exercises, analysis of headline units and banks, use of active verbs, avoiding infinitive misuse, punctuation rules (semicolons, figures), keyed lines, cross-line and stepped heads, and the concept of 'punch' in a head. Heads must be prepared with attention to linotype composition and page space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feature Story Requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Feature stories are dramatic, have a single effect, use color words, and often emphasize the particular and literary quality; the feature may omit a standard news lead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elements: a strong beginning, single effect or tone, vividness/color, and a climax. Exercises and short-model features are recommended; special-feature articles and short features are appropriate for high school papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial Writing (Point, Beginning, Body)
rubrics_metrics.description: An editorial has a clear point or thesis; its beginning and body must develop logical thinking to persuade or analyze public issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formula and plan of organization are provided; editorial cautions include clarity of argument and logical structure. Opinion is allowed and expected in editorials; exercises and models are provided, including timely essays and sports comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Informative Interview (Preparation and Economy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Informative interviews require planning beforehand (questions, persons to interview), economy in questioning, and specific organizational forms for the resulting story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conducting guidance: forms of discourse, cautions, and exercises. Emphasis on economy, selecting the informative elements for the lead and body, and testing via classroom drills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human-Interest Interview (Personality Focus)
rubrics_metrics.description: Human-interest interviews aim to reveal personality and stage business; plan to set and stage the interview to produce vivid direct discourse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes classification of interviews, pre- and post-interview tasks, cautions, use of direct/indirect discourse, and exercises. Models and practice suggested to develop skill in drawing out personality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speech Report: Before, During, After
rubrics_metrics.description: Speech reports require preparation (knowing speaker/context), note-taking during the speech, and careful recall and organization after the speech to form a lead and structured body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance covers form of discourse, how to recall a speaker's points, cautions about accuracy, and models/exercises for practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow-up and Latest Development Reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow-up stories must present the latest development and be organized so that the new or latest facts are prominent and connected to the original event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Play up a single element or the latest development; include ways to follow up and exercises/models for follow-up stories. Emphasize relation to the main event and clarity for readers who may not know the background.

rubrics_metrics.name: Background and Context
rubrics_metrics.description: Background material is used to give punch, grace, and context to stories and features; background may be used to produce clarity and reader understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Background is taught in relation to feature-writing and news — its appropriate placement and concise presentation are stressed. Use background to increase literary quality but avoid burying facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newspaper English: Clarity, Conciseness, Concreteness, Vividness
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspaper English emphasizes active verbs, short sentences, concrete and precise words, conciseness, vividness, and avoidance of passive voice and vague words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises and models illustrate use of active verbs, precise color words, avoiding generalities, keeping sentences short and concrete. Practice drills and keys are provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct vs Indirect Discourse (Quotations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use direct (quoted) discourse and indirect discourse deliberately; choose forms of discourse appropriate to interview, speech report, and feature needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance on how to present quotes, how to set dialogue or reported speech, and exercises comparing models of direct and indirect discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notebook, Files, Morgue and Source Management
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters must keep notebooks, files, and a morgue for background and sourcing; maintaining accessible records helps in follow-ups and features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical classroom suggestions for building sources and files, plus appendices listing high-school news sources. Emphasis on organized record-keeping for accuracy and follow-up reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make-up / Page Planning: Balance, Harmony, Variety, Dummy
rubrics_metrics.description: Page make-up must observe principles of balance, harmony, variety, and unity; a 'dummy' page should be prepared to plan headlines, art, copy placement and page flow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruction on planning front pages, making dummies, materials and schedules, use of symmetry/asymmetry, running heads, and models of New York Times pages. Exercises included for practical layout experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofreading and Copy-Editing Procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: There are established procedures for preparing copy, guide lines for linotype, symbol codes for copy reading, proof correction, galley proofs, and the proof-reader's code.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical steps: prepare copy for machine set, estimate length, correct and revise, use guide lines and symbols, read and mark galley proofs, and correct revised proofs. Appendix contains proof-reader codes and exercises in reading proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style Sheet / Consistency of Style
rubrics_metrics.description: A style sheet should be evolved and rigidly enforced for all writing; whatever the paper's in-house style is should be taught consistently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book presents a sample style sheet and advises teachers to enforce consistency. Exercises help students practice the sheet; evolution and adaptation to the school's needs are discussed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising Principles for School Papers
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertising should be planned with clear aims, imagination and appeal; campaigns (general and special), copy preparation, sizes, slogans, and rates must be considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance on advertising copy principles (appeal, personality, imagination), types of campaigns, placing and cutting ads, and practical advice on selling space and setting rates; models and exercises included.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sports Reporting Conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Sports reporting has its own conventions: timeliness, appropriate vernacular, forecasting, use of play-by-play, feature angles, and heads suited to sports copy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Directions for covering games, use of dope and forecasts, when to use vernacular, writing sports features and comment, and exercises modeling baseball, football, basketball and other sports copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviews (Books, Plays, Films, Music): Purpose and Points to Cover
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviews should state their aim (inform/persuade/evaluate) and cover key points relevant to the medium (collection/plot/performance/technical details), while avoiding mere generality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separate chapters on book reviewing, play-reviewing, film reviewing, and music criticism include cautions, models, and exercises. Advice covers framing the review, evidence for judgment, and concise, concrete commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Columns and Column Writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Columnists need a distinctive voice, economy, topicality, and organized content — columns should be planned for page continuity and reader appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hints for conducting columns, models, and exercises; instructions on running articles and exchanges. Emphasis on personality and regular features for maintaining readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judging Scale for Scholastic Newspapers
rubrics_metrics.description: An objective judging scale is provided for evaluating scholastic newspapers, including standards for organization, content, writing, headlines, make-up, and advertising.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appendix contains a judging scale and keys; teachers/advisers are advised to use such scales when evaluating student papers or compiling class assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogical Practices: Classroom Exercises and Oral Reading
rubrics_metrics.description: Students learn best by studying many short models and practicing writing; classroom practices include oral reading of models and student work, daily lead drills, and group correction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author prescribes that first few exercises in each chapter be done, suggests reading many leads in succession, writing leads on the board daily, and using keys to exercises for self-testing and teacher measurement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grammar and Sentence-Openings for Newspaper Writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Grammatical beginnings (noun, participial phrase, prepositional phrase, infinitive, nominal clauses, time clauses, nominative absolute) are taught as devices to vary openings and achieve clarity and emphasis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapters include exercises (45–48) on grammatical beginnings and guidance on their appropriate use in leads and features. Cautions about clarity and potential ambiguity accompany examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Names, Datelines and Identification
rubrics_metrics.description: Proper identification (names, datelines, who/what/where/when) must be used in leads and copies so readers can immediately grasp the facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples throughout show how to begin leads with datelines and names; guidance on what to identify in first sentences and how identification affects headline writing and reader comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding 'Rehashing' and Generalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid rehashing material and general, vague statements; prefer specific, lively facts and particulars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruction warns against lazy summarizing, recommends fresh angles and particulars, and provides exercises to turn rehashed material into vivid, specific copy.
